extracted.intended_audience: philanthropists, foundation trustees, institutional donors, philanthropic administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and operational standards for designing, endowing, administering, and adapting large charitable gifts and trusts (libraries, research institutions, pension funds, hero/pension funds, church gifts). Emphasizes trustee selection, fund purpose, administrative systems, beneficiary selection, matching contributions, and mechanisms to avoid misuse or perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define broad and explicit institutional purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "To encourage in the broadest and most liberal manner investigations, research and discovery, and the application of knowledge to the improvement of mankind; and, in particular, to conduct, endow and assist investigation in any department of science, literature or art, and to this end to coöperate with governments, universities, colleges, technical schools, learned societies, and individuals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a clear, large‑scale mission statement in the deed of gift that sets scope (research, education, art, science) and explicitly authorizes cooperation with governments, universities and other bodies so the institution's purpose is legally and publicly stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select distinguished, appropriate trustees and directors
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie named a body of "distinguished men" (e.g., Secretary of State, leading scientists, civic leaders) to serve as directors and first officers of institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose trustees with stature, expertise, and integrity to guard against misuse; consult leading public officials where appropriate (Carnegie consulted President Roosevelt and John Hay). A high‑quality governing board lends credibility and oversight to the gift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include governance flexibility (supermajority power to change objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie proposed that a majority should have the power to change objects but adopted the suggestion of not less than two thirds; "It is incorporated in all my large gifts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write into trust/deed a mechanism (e.g., two‑thirds of trustees) allowing adaptation of purposes and modes of applying funds so the gift can remain useful as circumstances change, while guarding against caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure endowment funding prudently and tie additions to demonstrated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: "I gave ten million dollars in five per cent bonds, to which there has been added sufficient to make the total cash value twenty‑five millions of dollars, the additions being made upon record of results obtained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use secure, income‑producing investments (e.g., bonds) as endowment core; consider conditional additional funding tied to measurable results or performance to encourage effective use of initial gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint committed, capable administrators (the right man in the right place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie found a president for the Hero Fund in Charlie Taylor, a devoted man who would not take a salary: "He is the right man in the right place."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select administrators or executive officers who are deeply committed, trustworthy, and competent; sometimes devotion and suitability matter more than formal compensation. Good administration is central to fund success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the fund's aim explicit to avoid perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: "A strange misconception arose at first... Many thought that its purpose was to stimulate heroic action... It is absurd. True heroes think not of reward. The fund is intended to pension or provide..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state whether a fund is a pension/relief mechanism (support for disabled or survivors) rather than a reward program, to avoid encouraging hazardous or otherwise undesirable behavior driven by financial incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize applications and graduate gifts according to need/size
rubrics_metrics.description: "Finally, however, a rigid system of giving was developed. A printed schedule requiring answers to many questions has now to be filled and returned before action is taken... we graduate the gift according to the size of the church."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standardized application forms and objective schedules to evaluate requests; scale gifts to the recipient's size and demonstrated need to ensure fairness and efficient allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require beneficiary contribution/matching to ensure stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding organs for churches: Carnegie asked each congregation to pay one half of the desired new organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require partial funding or matching contributions from beneficiaries (or local stakeholders) so recipients have commitment and oversight over expenditure and to reduce wasteful or extravagant requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve beneficiaries' dignity through anonymity and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: On private pension fund: "There is no publicity about it. No one knows who is embraced. Not a word is ever breathed to others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep certain charitable disbursements confidential to protect recipients' dignity, prevent dependence on publicity, and avoid creating resentments or social stigma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select beneficiaries on demonstrated deservingness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not one person have I ever placed upon the pension list that did not fully deserve assistance. It is a real roll of honor and mutual affection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish selection criteria emphasizing worthiness, demonstrated need, and personal knowledge or verified records; maintain a careful, principled beneficiary list to ensure funds go to deserving cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local commissions/committees and international coordination for funds spread across countries
rubrics_metrics.description: German Hero Fund: carefully chosen Commission corresponded with English and French Commissions, exchanged reports, and made plans to keep in touch; "They were deeply interested in the American report and have learned much from it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When operating in multiple jurisdictions, appoint carefully chosen local commissions, encourage cross‑commission communication and report exchange, and adapt practices to local conditions while sharing lessons learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target gifts where need is greatest (favor smaller institutions/colleges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie believed big universities were "large enough" and that smaller institutions (the colleges especially) were in greater need; he confined himself to aiding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize grants to institutions or areas where additional funding produces the most social good (e.g., smaller colleges, underfunded schools) rather than automatically expanding already large institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with other philanthropists and boards to avoid counterproductive overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie described later finding Mr. Rockefeller's General Education Board and noted: "Coöperation was soon found to be much to our mutual advantage, and we now work in unison."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate and coordinate with other major donors and philanthropic bodies to harmonize efforts, avoid duplication, and mitigate unintended negative outcomes from uncoordinated giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate instrument for the charitable objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie established a variety of instruments—public libraries, the Carnegie Institution, the Hero Fund, pension funds for professors, donations to colleges, organs for churches—each serving different aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the legal and organizational vehicle (endowment, pension fund, trust, grant program, prize/fund) to the specific social objective (research, education, pensions, rescue/hero support, cultural gifts) for greatest effectiveness.
